title: “We are not ship jumpers”, SODELPA GS tells PAP - The Fiji Times
content: SODELPA general secretary Levi Vere has hit out at the People’s Alliance Party (PAP), declaring that SODELPA does not need lessons on political loyalty because its members are not “ship jumpers”. Mr Vere accused PAP of attempting to lecture SODELPA on political timing and parliamentary numbers while overlooking the sacrifices made by the party during the Bainimarama administration. “We do not need lessons on loyalty because we are not ship jumpers,” Mr Vere said. He said SODELPA had stood virtually alone in opposing the Bainimarama government long before PAP emerged as a political party. “Long before PAP ever emerged as a political party, SODELPA stood virtually alone in the trenches fighting the Bainimarama regime.” Mr Vere claimed that since 2014, SODELPA members, particularly women and youths, had faced political persecution and public humiliation for defending indigenous rights. “Since 2014, while today’s so-called political champions were silent, compromised, or nowhere to be seen, SODELPA’s members, our youth, and our mothers paid dearly,” he said. “Our people faced political persecution, were hauled before the courts, and were shamed publicly for standing up for indigenous rights.” He also credited SODELPA with leading opposition to the former government’s proposal to change Fiji’s national flag. “Our youths and women fought the Bainimarama regime when it wanted to change our national flag,” he said. “SODELPA led the fight that saved our national flag and identity!” Mr Vere maintained that the party’s political standing was built on years of struggle rather than political convenience. “SODELPA earned its mandate through blood, sweat, tears, and relentless sacrifice—not through political convenience.” His comments come amid political differences between SODELPA and PAP over constitutional reform and parliamentary support.

title: Sölden Men’s GS 2026: Pinheiro Braathen Wins, Radamus Fourth - Ski Racing Media
content: Lucas Pinheiro Braathen, Marco Odermatt / GEPA pictures Three of the final four racers took the lead. The last man down the mountain won. Brazil’s Lucas Pinheiro Braathen delivered a commanding victory in Sunday’s Sölden men’s World Cup giant slalom, defeating Switzerland’s Loïc Meillard and Marco Odermatt in a thrilling opening to the 2026-27 season. The reigning Olympic and World Cup GS champion entered the second run with a 0.24-second advantage. What followed was an extraordinary battle on the Rettenbach glacier. American River Radamus held the leader’s chair deep into the final seven before three of the last four starters took turns moving into first place. Pinheiro Braathen eventually prevailed by 0.48 seconds, while just one hundredth separated the two Swiss podium finishers. The reverse-30 second run had already produced remarkable performances and several lead changes before the leading contenders prepared to challenge. Radamus, who had started the afternoon tied for 15th, remained the overall leader when only seven racers were left. His exceptional second run had forced the biggest names in giant slalom to chase his time. Henrik Kristoffersen, seventh after Run 1, couldn’t find the necessary speed and eventually finished 22nd. Germany’s Fabian Gratz also fell short of Radamus’ mark. Norway’s Atle Lie McGrath, fifth after the opening run, fell on the upper pitch and failed to finish. Odermatt, fourth after Run 1, delivered the seventh-fastest second run. The Swiss star finally ended Radamus’ extended stay in the leader’s chair. “I made a big step in the second run: I found the race gear and that’s the most important thing,” Odermatt told FIS. His third-place finish would ultimately become his 47th World Cup GS podium, establishing a Swiss record. It was an encouraging start after an offseason affected by injury. Austria’s Stefan Brennsteiner was next. Third after the opening run, Brennsteiner couldn’t match the pace. His second run ranked 22nd, dropping him to 11th overall and guaranteeing Odermatt a podium. The Swiss skier had finished the first run 0.31 seconds ahead of his teammate. He needed to protect that advantage to take the lead. Although Odermatt recorded a faster second run, Meillard delivered a strong finishing section and crossed just 0.01 seconds ahead. The result was especially satisfying for Meillard, who had never previously finished higher than fifth at Sölden. “Sölden and me haven’t been friends in the last few years so to start the season with a podium and some solid skiing feels good,” Meillard told FIS. The narrow margin over his teammate added another layer of satisfaction. “I had a few times when I was one-hundredth behind, so now it’s my turn to be in the front,” Meillard said. Odermatt recognized that the ultimate challenge remained the Brazilian who had dominated the opening run. “Lucas was too fast in the first run for the victory today,” he acknowledged afterward. Meillard had the lead. Odermatt was guaranteed third. Lucas Pinheiro Braathen, the reigning Olympic and World Cup GS champion, stood at the start knowing the entire race would be decided by his final run. Lucas Pinheiro Braathen stood at the start knowing he was the only racer who could deny Meillard victory. The 26-year-old Brazilian had already established himself as the world’s leading giant slalom racer, winning Olympic GS gold and the discipline’s World Cup crystal globe last season. Pinheiro Braathen had dominated the shortened first run, opening a 0.24-second advantage over Meillard and a 0.55-second lead over Odermatt. The same reduced course length was used for Run 2. Both runs had become intense sprints, with less accumulated fatigue but little opportunity to recover lost time. He increased his overall advantage through the opening and middle sections, reaching the final sector with 0.61 seconds in hand over Meillard. The Swiss skier had been particularly strong on the closing stretch, and Pinheiro Braathen surrendered some of his advantage approaching the finish. Pinheiro Braathen crossed 0.48 seconds clear, securing his fifth World Cup giant slalom victory and 12th podium in the discipline. His second-run time ranked 10th fastest. Combined with his exceptional opening performance, however, it was more than enough. Three of the final four racers had taken the lead. The final starter had won. Pinheiro Braathen acknowledged the expectations he carried into Sölden. “There was a lot of pressure on my shoulders today,” he said in his finish-area interview. “Pressure is privilege, and I was able to capitalize off of that.” The victory marked a remarkable contrast to the previous year’s Sölden opener, when Pinheiro Braathen failed to finish. This time, the Atomic and Oakley athlete arrived as the reigning Olympic champion and World Cup GS titleholder. “What a relief to be able to open the show in this way,” he said. Pinheiro Braathen explained that he had spent the offseason searching for new ways to improve following his Olympic gold and crystal globe. Those achievements brought confidence rather than hesitation. “I didn’t want to hesitate. I knew what I had in me,” he said. The Brazilian also thanked his family, team and supporters, recognizing their contribution to his latest victory. For the United States, River Radamus delivered one of the most impressive performances of the afternoon. The only Stifel U.S. Ski Team racer to qualify for the second run, Radamus finished the opening run tied for 15th, 1.15 seconds behind Pinheiro Braathen. “I was disappointed in my first run because I don’t think that I showed the skiing that I’ve been working towards,” Radamus said afterward. With some of the pressure lifted, the American attacked and produced a time of 51.99 seconds, the second fastest of the afternoon. Only Austria’s Raphael Haaser, who recorded 51.90, skied faster. “But the pressure was off a bit the second run, and I was able to connect some of the good turns that I’ve been working on,” Radamus said. “I’m happy with the progress we’re showing.” The American was particularly effective through the middle sector, where he posted the fastest time in the field. Against Haaser, who was leading when Radamus started, he built a 0.45-second advantage by the final intermediate split. Radamus lost 0.41 seconds of that cushion on the final stretch but crossed just 0.04 seconds ahead of the Austrian. One challenger after another failed to beat his combined time of 1:45.54. When the final seven racers prepared to start, Radamus was still leading. His performance had transformed the race, forcing the sport’s biggest stars to beat a time established by a racer who had finished the opening run in 15th. Eleven subsequent starters failed to displace him before Odermatt finally took the lead. Radamus ultimately finished fourth, climbing 11 positions and missing the podium by 0.33 seconds. Radamus offered valuable insight into why the second run produced so many impressive climbs. “The course was almost the exact same,” he said. “We were in the same grooves for a lot of it, so we knew what to expect.” The shortened course featured relatively open turns, allowing racers to maintain speed and attack. “It was very easy, very open. The snow was great,” Radamus explained. “You couldn’t afford to slow yourself down at all. You had to go at it.” That approach proved particularly effective for racers who had started the afternoon outside the leading group. Radamus also acknowledged that conditions changed between runs. The snow became more mixed, while visibility and wind remained considerations on the mountain. “The snow changed a bit between runs. It was like sort of a spring mix in the second run,” he said. Rather than dwell on the changing conditions, Radamus focused on making the most of them. “I tried to take advantage and make the most of it.” His result provided an outstanding start to the season. Radamus said he planned to remain in Europe for super-G training before returning to the United States to prepare for the upcoming World Cup races at Copper Mountain. Britain’s Freddy Carrick-Smith provided another of the afternoon’s memorable performances. The 19-year-old started the opening run wearing bib 46 and qualified for his first World Cup second run in a tie for 21st place. That achievement alone was significant for British alpine racing. His afternoon performance made the occasion even more memorable. Carrick-Smith produced the fifth-fastest second run, stopping the clock at 52.21 seconds. He climbed nine positions to finish 12th, earning his first World Cup points. “Yeah, it was amazing,” Carrick-Smith said afterward. “I guess I couldn’t have asked for much more out of my first run and second run.” The young Briton acknowledged that finishing his second run had been a priority. He held back slightly rather than risk losing the opportunity. Even so, his competitive time ranked among the day’s strongest performances. His breakthrough recalls fellow British racer Charlie Raposo’s World Cup giant slalom results at Kranjska Gora in March 2022. For a teenager competing against the world’s best, 12th place represents a significant career milestone. Carrick-Smith also spoke about representing a country with relatively few World Cup alpine competitors. “There’s not many GB skiers. It’s just good to be an influence, I guess.” Austria’s Raphael Haaser delivered the fastest second run of the competition, recording 51.90 seconds. Starting the afternoon in 20th, Haaser climbed 15 places to finish fifth, just 0.04 seconds behind Radamus. France’s Léo Anguenot also enjoyed a remarkable afternoon. The French racer temporarily occupied the leader’s chair before finishing ninth, improving 14 places from his first-run position. Norway’s Rasmus Bakkevig, the reigning Junior World GS champion, delivered another exceptional performance. Starting with bib 49, Bakkevig qualified 29th in the opening run. He then produced the fourth-fastest second run, taking an early lead and holding it through five subsequent challengers. He eventually finished 14th, climbing 15 positions. Six athletes moved up at least 10 places during the second run. Finland’s Eduard Hallberg earns the Ski Racing Media Bibbo Award, recognizing the greatest numerical improvement from original starting bib to final finishing position. Hallberg started with bib 55 and finished 16th, a difference of 39 positions. The Finn also recorded the fastest final sector of the second run, demonstrating impressive speed over the closing stretch. Bakkevig deserves recognition as well. The young Norwegian started bib 49 and finished 14th, a difference of 35 positions. Both performances illustrate the opportunities available to racers starting deep in the field. Switzerland left Sölden with two podium finishers, while Norway failed to place a racer in the top 10 despite qualifying six athletes for the second run. For a nation accustomed to success in men’s giant slalom, the absence of a Norwegian among the leaders was unusual. Kristoffersen dropped from seventh to 22nd, while Lie McGrath failed to finish. However, Norway’s younger athletes delivered encouraging performances. Eirik Hystad Solberg climbed from 13th to eighth, while Bakkevig’s remarkable second run demonstrated the potential of the next generation. Germany also showed improving depth in giant slalom. Three German racers qualified for the second run. Gratz finished sixth, Grammel climbed from 30th to 15th, and Alexander Schmid placed 21st. Norway led all nations with six second-run qualifiers. Austria and Switzerland each qualified four, while seven nations had just one racer advance. The 2026-27 World Cup giant slalom season opened with seven overall lead changes, remarkable climbs and an extraordinary battle among the final four racers. But when the competition reached its decisive moment, the reigning champion delivered. Pinheiro Braathen defeated two of Switzerland’s most accomplished racers and demonstrated that last season’s Olympic gold and crystal globe had not diminished his ambition. The Brazilian opened the season with victory, leaving his rivals with an immediate challenge: finding a way to beat the world’s leading giant slalom racer. Special thanks to Ski Racing Media journalist Darka Sefcik Starnova for her on-site reporting in Sölden and finish-area interviews, bringing the athletes’ voices and perspectives directly into this story. Darka Sefcik Starnova has loved ski racing since childhood, when she also competed in children’s categories. She founded United Ski Fans as a safe space for alpine ski racing enthusiasts, both online and at the races. Through this project, she shares engaging content from the world of fandom, fan clubs, and grandstand fun — simply for the joy of it. Darka is especially dedicated to the fan clubs of Petra Vlhová and Lucas Pinheiro Braathen. She believes alpine skiing is a sport of love, where fans treat each other with kindness and many athletes serve as role models for the younger generation. In her professional life, Darka works in education, where she values healthy and positive role models just as strongly. title: The Cheapest Adventure Bikes With More Than 100 Horsepower - HotCars
content: Today, the adventure bike market is almost as diverse as the industry itself, with a wide range of bikes that will appeal to pretty much every kind of rider. While there is a growing contingent of riders gravitating towards lighter, more off-road oriented machines, there are still several great adventure-tourers on the market that will appeal to those looking for something more comfortable and powerful. All these bikes offer a semblance of off-road potential, but bigger, more powerful engines most certainly weigh more, and once you reach a certain weight class, serious off-roading is more or less off the table. Realistically speaking, most riders are not buying an ADV for that purpose, they will primarily be using them for long distance travel, and that is where all these bikes shine. Offering more comfort and features than some dedicated touring bikes. Most modern bikes share engines. For the sake of variety, we limited it to one model per platform. We are still struggling to unpack exactly how MV Agusta is able to price the Enduro Veloce like this for the US market. We can only assume that they are betting on selling enough of them to make up for whatever profit is lost on each model. These bikes come fully equipped with all the adventure-touring toys, from those hard cases to IMU-backed electronics. In an effort to win back some semblance of consumer confidence, these bikes come with a 5-year warranty ... if MV will still be around for that long. It is worth remembering that this is a company that simply rolls from one financial crisis to another. Unlike MV, who seem determined to live out every conceivable Italian cliché known to man, Ducati has long since found a way to build more reliable bikes without losing their identity. One of the more recent reliability-centered decisions was ditching desmodromic valves for certain models, and the DesertX is one of them. While desmo has its place in high-performance models, conventional variable valve timing is most certainly a better, more practical choice for this middleweight ADV. A third Italian bike in as many entries may leave some ADV enthusiasts scratching their heads, but the Stelvio’s unconventional transverse V-twin delivers an impressive 115 horsepower. Piaggio’s flagship ADV continues to get upstaged by the Aprilia Tuareg 660, though, and it is pretty easy to see the appeal of the lighter “brother from another mother.” For those looking for a more comfortable long distance tourer, the Stelvio is most certainly worth the extra outlay. Suzuki has a knack for making the most out of older engines and the big V-Strom is no exception. This twin can trace its roots all the way back to the infamous TL1000S (and TL1000R sport bike). While it has been reworked to better suit the ADV, it is still a fun, tractable engine that belies the rather uninspiring design of the bike. At least the V-Strom won’t suddenly lose its rear end like the old TL1000S! For all those KTM enthusiasts screaming at the screen, the Norden 901 is cheaper, and an objectively better looking bike. It certainly lacks the off-road capability of the 890 Adventure R (which really is remarkable for its size) but if that is really what you are after, then it might actually be worth considering the new 690 Rally, which is even cheaper than the Norden, but not even in the same conversation when it comes to long-distance comfort. When compared to the aforementioned V-Strom 1050, we have always found the Africa Twin surprisingly affordable. The base model is more off-road oriented, but at the end of the day, this is still a 500 pound motorcycle, and off-road, it will handle like a 500 pound motorcycle. Along with being surprisingly affordable, it is also surprisingly comfortable. What is not surprising at all is the fact that it is as reliable as any Honda product, so peace of mind is simply part of the deal. The base model Tiger 900 is more street oriented than any of the other 900s, and while you still reserve the right to go off-road with more confidence than the average street bike, it is more of a tourer. It is an exceptionally comfortable bike, and like most triples, it offers the best of both worlds in terms of performance, with the grunt of a twin and high RPM performance of an inline-four. Also, like most triples, you will get some vibrations through the bars at highway speed. It will bother some, and won’t fuss others. A test ride is essential! Upon first inspection, the F 900 GS looks like a bit of a bargain. The base model already comes with an Akrapovič exhaust, and it offers the most off-road potential out of all these 100-ish horsepower ADVs (the DesertX might have something to say about this), but with BMW there is always a “but.” Even the paint you see in this photo will cost extra, and so will several other features that really shouldn’t be optional at this price point. China has arrived to the big bore ADV party in the most Italian way possible. While Moto Morini bikes are all built in China, they are also designed in Italy, and it shows, because the X-Cape family are among the best looking adventure bikes on the market. This V-twin was also developed in Italy (albeit some two decades ago) before the company was absorbed by its Chinese parent, and makes a healthy 129 horsepower. The Ibex 950’s arrival is unusually quiet compared to the excitement that surrounded the lightweight 450. It features an uprated version of the KTM LC8c parallel twin which now makes 112 horsepower. Only time will tell if it still has the same appetite for cams as the version found in the aforementioned Norden, but if CFMoto has solved that problem, this might be the ADV deal of the year. If there was any suggestion that Lucas Pinheiro Braathen (BRA/Atomic) would suffer a letdown this season after his extraordinary success earlier this year, those fears have been put to rest at the first time of asking. The Brazilian won the season-opening Giant Slalom race in Sölden on Sunday, marking his fourth straight elite GS victory, including his Olympic triumph and the late-season wins that propelled him to the 2026 Crystal Globe. Leading after the first run, Pinheiro Braathen skied aggressively but calmly in the second run to cruise to a deserved victory by nearly half a second over Loïc Meillard (SUI/Rossignol, +0.48s) and Marco Odermatt (SUI/Stöckli, +0.49s). "There was a lot of pressure on my shoulders today," Pinheiro Braathen said, referencing the beginning of his title defense and the highly-anticipated resumption of his rivalry with former GS king Odermatt. "But pressure is privilege and I was able to capitalize on that. What a relief to be able to open the show in this way." After returning to the tour two years ago with Brazil following a year in retirement after his early career with Norway, the 26-year-old has methodically ticked off a series of firsts for the nation he now represents: first World Cup win, first Winter Olympic medal (and gold at that), first Crystal Globe. Having reached those dizzying heights in such a short time, the philosophical Pinheiro Braathen put a lot of thought over the off-season into what would come next. "I've been searching for new curiosities, new paths to evolve from last year's Olympic gold and the Globe," he said. "We're headed towards new goals, new objectives." Yet he produced the same brilliant skiing that has repeatedly propeled him to the top of the podium in recent times. When he crossed the finish line in first place, he emphatically yelled "Vamos!" into the camera. "Even already from the second half of last season, I was able to bring that freedom that came with being able to accomplish those results, and bring that spirit into the very first race (on Sunday)," he said. "I didn't want to hesitate, I knew what I had in me, and I'm so, so proud to put it out there." On a bumpy, windy course from the reserve state gate that reduced each run to under a minute, there was no room for errors or hesitation even as the skiers were trying to find the snow under their feet in their first race of the season. While Pinheiro Braathen mastered the conditions the best, the Swiss pair of Meillard and Odermatt showed they are not far from the top of their game, even at this early stage of the season. Meillard, in particular, tends to start slowly and work his way into the season, and he had never finished higher than fifth on the Rettenbach glacier before Sunday. "Sölden and me haven't been friends in the last few years so to start the season with a podium and some solid skiing feels good," he said. As the second-last skier on the mountain, he trailed provisional leader Odermatt at the final intermediate split, but used a scintillating closeout to overtake his teammate by the barest of margins in ski racing: one-hundredth of a second. "I had a few times when I was one-hundredth behind, so now it's my turn to be in the front," Meillard said. "I guess next race, it's him again, and that's the beauty of the sport." Odermatt, the four-time Giant Slalom title winner who lost his Olympic gold and his Crystal Globe to Pinheiro Braathen last season, was satisfied with third after having his pre-season affected by injury. "To start the season with a podium is always nice," he said. "I made a big step in the second run: I found the race gear and that's the most important thing." Odermatt's 47th World Cup Giant Slalom podium moved him ahead of Michael Von Gruenigen (SUI) and Vreni Schneider (SUI) for the most all-time among Swiss racers, and that podium was about the most he could have hoped for on this day. "Lucas was too fast in the first run for the victory today," Odermatt admitted. For Pinheiro Braathen, it was his second victory in Sölden after he triumphed in 2020 while racing for Norway, and the personal journey he has undertaken between those wins was not lost on him. "It's amazing to look back at being able to be the youngest winner here and to come and do it again," he said. "That's something very special for me. That very day here, when I was 20 years old, that changed my life." Six years later, racing under a different flag and with new perspectives on skiing and life, it all came together for the Brazilian on Sunday. "I was just able to be me, I was able to be so connected with myself, and it felt so fun to ski that second run," he said. "I knew that this was how I was supposed to feel. And that's the feeling that I chase every single day.

title: Sölden Men’s GS 2026: Pinheiro Braathen Leads Run 1 - Ski Racing Media
content: Lucas Pinheiro Braathen returned to Sölden on Sunday, Oct. 25, and delivered the fastest first run of the men’s 2026-27 Alpine World Cup opener. Behind him, seven racers starting bib 31 or higher fought their way into the second run, transforming the battle for qualification. A year after failing to finish the opening giant slalom on the Rettenbach glacier, the Brazilian Olympic champion and reigning World Cup GS titleholder showed exactly why he enters the new season as the skier to beat. Racing on Atomic skis and wearing Oakley eyewear, Pinheiro Braathen clocked 52.40 seconds. Switzerland’s Loïc Meillard finished just 0.24 seconds behind, while Austria’s Stefan Brennsteiner took third at +0.49. Defending Sölden champion Marco Odermatt sits fourth, 0.55 behind the leader, setting up an intriguing second-run battle. Strong winds forced organizers to start at the top of the steep pitch, shortening the first run to about 53 seconds. Overcast skies reduced visibility, and organizers removed the usual banner above the finish due to wind concerns. U.S.-born Norwegian Atle Lie McGrath, racing on HEAD skis, became the first man to start a World Cup race in the new season. Austrian Stefan Brennsteiner quickly set a faster benchmark before his teammate, Marco Schwarz, disappointed the home crowd with an early mistake that ended his run. Schwartz said, “Conditions are great, no issue, good work. I just wanted to be in a very straight line and it didn’t work.” Starting fourth, the Brazilian delivered the fastest middle sector and established a lead that survived all 69 starters. Meillard offered the closest challenge. After struggling to find his best form early last season, the Swiss star produced an encouraging performance. He matched the fastest opening-sector time but surrendered most of his 0.24-second deficit near the finish. Odermatt, racing on Stöckli skis and Salomon boots, remained within striking distance but lost 0.29 seconds in the middle sector alone. Henrik Kristoffersen provided another revealing contrast. The Norwegian matched the fastest opening split but lost 0.58 seconds in the final sector, leaving him seventh. The opening group established the early contenders, but improving visibility soon created opportunities for the racers starting behind them. As the light improved, several later starters demonstrated that the early leaders were not beyond reach. Germany’s Fabian Gratz, wearing bib 10, moved into sixth. Then Italy’s Giovanni Borsotti delivered one of the morning’s strongest performances, charging into eighth from bib 29, just 0.79 seconds behind Pinheiro Braathen. Germany’s Alexander Schmid followed from bib 27, finishing ninth at +0.84. France’s Thibaut Favrot, starting 21st, claimed 10th after producing a final sector just 0.01 seconds slower than the leader. Croatia’s Filip Zubčić also offered an encouraging sign. After a difficult season and a switch to Nordica skis and Marker bindings, the proven GS contender finished 12th, only 0.98 seconds behind. Belgium’s Sam Maes, who trains with the Stifel U.S. Ski Team and races on Völkl skis, finished 11th at +0.92. River Radamus was the lone American to qualify, finishing tied for 15th, 1.15 seconds behind Pinheiro Braathen. The Stifel U.S. Ski Team racer initially crossed in 10th but gradually slipped as later starters delivered faster performances. Radamus has demonstrated the ability to produce exceptionally fast individual runs, leaving him an opportunity to attack in the afternoon. Great Britain’s 19-year-old Freddy Carrick-Smith delivered an even more dramatic performance. Starting bib 46, the young British racer charged into a tie for 21st, just 1.37 seconds behind the leader. He finished 25 positions ahead of his starting number, securing a rare World Cup giant slalom second run for Britain. The achievement recalls Charlie Raposo’s performance at Kranjska Gora in March 2022, when the British racer advanced to the second run and finished 27th. No Canadian, Japanese or South Korean racers qualified. The final starting group delivered one of the morning’s biggest surprises. With only one of the opening 30 racers failing to finish, opportunities appeared limited for those starting farther back. Yet seven racers wearing bib 31 or higher qualified for the second run, displacing several established competitors. Improving visibility helped create opportunities, but these athletes still needed exceptional execution to capitalize. Fastest high-bib qualifier: Sandvik, who finished 18th from bib 32. Highest bib to qualify: Hallberg, who started 55th and finished 26th. Biggest improvement: Hallberg also made the largest move, gaining 29 positions relative to his starting number. Italy’s Franzoni provided another remarkable highlight. Despite losing a full second in the middle sector, he produced the fastest final sector of the entire field, beating Pinheiro Braathen’s split by 0.13 seconds. The battle for qualification proved unforgiving. Ryder Sarchett of the Stifel U.S. Ski Team initially moved into 27th from bib 34, but later finishers pushed him outside the top 30. Seven successful high-bib qualifiers demonstrated the depth of the field and ensured that the opening race delivered drama well beyond the fight for the lead. The fastest 30 return in reverse order, with Pinheiro Braathen starting last. The Brazilian holds the advantage, but Meillard, Brennsteiner and Odermatt remain close enough to challenge. After a first run filled with surprises, the fight for the season’s opening World Cup victory is far from decided. title: From Sarah G’s ‘Tala’ to BINI hit: Thomasian PT turns music producer - The Varsitarian
content: LONG BEFORE producing hits for some of the country’s biggest pop artists, Julius “Jumbo” De Belen worked as a physical therapist. He eventually pursued his passion for music, becoming the producer of hits such as Sarah Geronimo’s “Tala” and BINI’s “Pantropiko.” De Belen graduated from the UST College of Rehabilitation Sciences (CRS) in 2003, having initially pursued physical therapy at his parents’ urging. “It’s more of my parents’ choice because they wanted someone in the family to be in the medical field,” De Belen told the Varsitarian. “I also wanted to challenge myself to be different from my brothers.” Although physical therapy was unrelated to his interest in music, he continued to pursue his passion. During his time at the University, when music was still a hobby, he formed a metal band with his friends called Joint. De Belen and his band joined “Fit and Tempo,” a now-defunct band competition held during the annual CRS Week. “There were contests like Battle of the Bands and competitions for original compositions, where I always joined. That was the only outlet back then, since there really wasn’t anything that connected music to physical therapy,” he said. His interest in music was encouraged by his mother, who provided him with instruments, including a bass guitar, electric guitars, and a drum set. Before forming Joint, he had established a band in high school and written his first song, “Karimlan,” in 1996. After graduating, he worked full-time as a physical therapist and eventually saved enough to buy his first equipment and begin producing music. He devoted his spare time to practicing and improving his production skills. He eventually began selling beats to establish himself as an emerging music producer. “People were helping me out by buying beats from me for 2,000 pesos,” De Belen recalled. “And it just happened that there were artists, especially rappers, who were going to my home studio, asking me to make music for them.” In 2009, he founded the music production company and record label FlipMusic with fellow UST alumnus Pow Chavez and Jellica Mateo, the label’s current chief executive officer. His career gained wider recognition when FlipMusic began collaborating with entertainment company Viva. In 2014, De Belen produced the soundtrack for the romantic comedy film “Diary ng Panget,” starring James Reid and Nadine Lustre. A defining moment in his career came in 2015, when he heard “Fly Away,” a song he produced for hip-hop duo Blaze N Kane and Pow Chavez, played on the radio. “There’s nothing more defining than hearing yourself get legitimized and be on air for the first time. The first time I heard that song, it actually made me cry,” De Belen said. He also helped fellow alumna Sarah Geronimo transition from ballads to pop music, producing her hits “Ikot-Ikot” in 2013 and “Tala” in 2015. During former vice president Maria Leonor “Leni” Robredo’s presidential campaign in 2022, FlipMusic produced the campaign songs “Kay Leni Tayo” and “Rosas.” For De Belen, producing the songs was a way of taking a stand. “Taking a side is really a hard thing to do because politics is always polarized. And sometimes, you have to take a stand,” De Belen said. “Show your ideas and express where your heart is.” That same year, he was invited to South Korea to learn more about K-pop, whose production techniques influenced his work on songs such as “Karera,” “Pantropiko” and “Salamin, Salamin” for the girl group BINI. The following year, BINI performed at the UST Quadricentennial Pavilion and Grandstand for the Welcome Concert and Paskuhan Concert. “It’s very heartwarming. Nakakatuwa na there’s a Thomasian responsible for the music that the new generation and the school were enjoying,” he said. (It is heartwarming to know that a Thomasian is responsible for the music enjoyed by the new generation and the University community.) De Belen attributed his success to persistence and hard work, encouraging aspiring musicians to continue pursuing their interests despite the industry’s challenges. “You have to really continue with the grit and grain. It’s hard to really put out songs, but if you persist in hard work, you know it pays off,” he said. This site uses Akismet to reduce spam. Learn how your comment data is processed.

title: Sölden Men’s GS 2026: Start List, Rankings, Times & How to Watch - Ski Racing Media
content: Lucas Pinheiro Braathen, Atle Lie McGrath / Sölden 2026 / GEPA pictures Lucas Pinheiro Braathen left Sölden last October without finishing the first run. By the end of the season, he owned the two biggest prizes available in giant slalom. The Brazilian won Olympic GS gold, captured the 2025-26 World Cup giant slalom title and closed the season with consecutive victories in Lillehammer and Kranjska Gora. Now Braathen returns to the Rettenbach glacier as the No. 1 skier on the GS World Cup Start List. The Atomic and Oakley athlete starts bib 4 Sunday and enters the 2026-27 opener as the man everyone else must beat. Defending Sölden champion Marco Odermatt starts bib 6, while Atle Lie McGrath opens the race with bib 1. The first men’s World Cup race of the season features 69 competitors from 24 nations. Pinheiro Braathen’s history with Sölden has taken several turns. He earned his first World Cup victory here in 2020 while representing Norway. Four years later, Sölden was where he scored Brazil’s first Alpine World Cup points. Last season brought another dramatic chapter. Pinheiro Braathen failed to finish the first run in Sölden, then produced the most successful GS season of his career. He won Brazil’s first Alpine World Cup Crystal Globe and brought the country its first Winter Olympic medal — and first gold — with his victory in the Milano Cortina giant slalom. He then won the final two World Cup giant slaloms in Lillehammer and Kranjska Gora. Pinheiro Braathen arrives on Sunday with five consecutive World Cup GS podiums and eight consecutive top-10 GS finishes. His World Cup career began with Norway, but his move to Brazil provided the path for him to continue racing after his break with the Norwegian system. He is now fully representing Brazil and has become one of the country’s most prominent winter-sport athletes. The Stöckli / Salomon skier won last year’s opener and has now won Sölden three times — in 2021, 2022 and 2025. A fourth victory on Sunday would tie American Ted Ligety for the most men’s World Cup GS wins in Sölden. Odermatt also makes his 200th World Cup start Sunday. He enters the season with 54 career World Cup victories and 102 podiums. His 29 career GS victories place him third on the men’s all-time list in the discipline. Braathen ended Odermatt’s run of four consecutive GS globes last winter. Their renewed battle begins immediately. The World Cup Start List and the current-season World Cup standings are different. The WCSL uses rolling results from previous races and helps determine start-order position. Because Sölden is the first giant slalom of 2026-27, there are no current-season GS standings yet. The top seven on the WCSL start Sunday in this bib order: Only four nations — Norway, Austria, Brazil and Switzerland — occupy the first seven WCSL positions. Switzerland and Norway have combined for 11 of the last 15 Sölden men’s GS podium positions. Odermatt won a tight race last October. The first four finished within four-tenths of a second. Radamus finished fourth in Sölden in 2024 and remains the highest-ranked American on the current GS WCSL. Sarchett earned his first World Cup GS top-10 last season when he finished 10th in Val d’Isère. Kenney enters the season with a different status and different equipment. He is an independent athlete competing as a Stifel U.S. Ski Team programmed athlete. He is coached by and trains with the U.S. team, but he is not a named team member and pays his own expenses. Kenney switched from Völkl/Marker to HEAD for this season and remains a SHRED athlete. Tommy Ford remains injured and will not race in Sölden. Sunday will be Paul Epstein’s first World Cup race as head coach of the Stifel U.S. Ski Team men’s technical program. Epstein previously ran the independent Global Racing program. That history creates an interesting connection inside Sunday’s race. Patrick Kenney raced with Global during his career. So did Belgium’s Sam Maes. Maes is now training with the Stifel U.S. Ski Team, giving American fans another athlete to follow this winter. Maes finished a career-best 12th in the World Cup GS standings last season. He recorded three top-seven finishes after never previously finishing inside the World Cup top seven. Read enters the season pursuing an 11th consecutive year scoring World Cup GS points. Sunday will also be his 204th World Cup start, moving him into fourth among Canadian Alpine racers, men and women combined, for career World Cup starts. Read has made seven previous Sölden starts. He has qualified for the second run four times and posted a career-best Sölden result of seventh in 2019. Carrick-Smith made his World Cup debut in last season’s Sölden giant slalom and returns for another opportunity on the Rettenbach glacier. Ski Racing Media has a significant and growing audience in Asia, particularly Japan and China. That makes Sunday’s late starters from Korea and Japan especially worth following. Both will attack from deep in the field, where adapting to changing course and snow conditions becomes increasingly important. Alexander Steen Olsen had been expected to make his World Cup return in Sölden after missing the entire 2025-26 season. Steen Olsen told Viaplay Norway that he had strongly hoped to race but concluded that he had not had enough preparation. “I’m a bit rusty on my skiing — I simply need more time,” he said. The Norwegian said he felt relieved after finally making the decision. He had been determined to start as long as his knee allowed it, but after missing an entire season, he decided more preparation was the better choice. Steen Olsen won the Sölden GS in 2024 and finished fourth in the season-long GS standings that winter. His immediate goal is now another training block before potentially returning in Levi. Odermatt returns to a hill where he has won three times. Pinheiro Braathen returns to the hill where he failed to finish a year ago — now carrying Olympic gold, the World Cup GS globe and the No. 1 WCSL ranking. Lie McGrath starts first. Brennsteiner follows with bib 2. Schwarz has bib 3. Then come Pinheiro Braathen, Meillard, Odermatt and Kristoffersen. The season begins immediately, with the world’s best giant slalom racers poised to attack. United States: Peacock will stream both runs live and on demand, with additional coverage on NBCSN. Watch Run 1 on Peacock and Run 2 on Peacock. A free full-race replay will be available on the Ski & Snowboard World Cup YouTube channel 24 hours after airing. title: FC Seoul Clinches 10-Year Title with GS Chairman's Motivation - 조선일보
content: Chairman Huh Tae-soo's Fan-First Initiatives Help Club Achieve Record Attendance and Championship [Sangam = Sports Chosun Reporter Kim Ga-eul] Huh Tae-soo, chairman of GS Group, has become the 'championship fairy.' FC Seoul, led by manager Kim Ki-dong, drew 1-1 with Gangwon FC in the final regular league match of the 'Hana Bank K League 1 2026' held at Seoul World Cup Stadium on the 24th. Seoul recorded 21 wins, 6 draws, and 6 losses. At the same time, second-place Ulsan HD also drew 2-2 with Pohang Steelers, bringing the championship race to a close. Seoul erased the three-point gap to the champion and clinched the title for the first time in 10 years since 2016. Including the Anyang LG era, this is the club's seventh 'star.' A special guest was present at the stadium: Huh Tae-soo, chairman of GS Group. It was a clear motivation for the team. Captain Kim Jin-su said, "I sincerely appreciate the chairman’s visit. It’s true that his presence motivated us even more. With the championship right in front of us, I think that motivation was greater for us than for any other players today," adding, "As someone representing the team, we obviously achieved the desired result, so I expect a generous bonus. I believe the chairman will surely recognize our hard work." After the match, Chairman Huh said, "During my last visit, I asked for a healthy season without injuries. You responded with a championship after 10 years. I applaud your efforts and want to share today’s joy with the fans who have longed for this victory." He has consistently emphasized 'Fan first,' focusing on improving fan services such as the club’s mobile app, customer-oriented merchandise, and stadium facilities. Seoul surpassed an average attendance of 22,000 people in the league this season, achieving success in both performance and fandom. Sangam = Reporter Kim Ga-eul epi17@sportschosun.com

title: Moltzan wins after Shiffrin fades, first GS podium for Aicher - Yahoo Sports
content: American Paula Moltzan claimed a first World Cup career win and Germany's Emma Aicher reached a first giant slalom podium in third on Saturday as superstar Mikaela Shiffrin and others faded in deteriorating conditions. Moltzan shot from fifth after the first run to the top of the podium at the season opener on the Sölden glacier, pipping Lara Colturi, who missed a first ever World Cup victory for Albania, by one-hundredths of a second. Aicher was .52 back in third. Shiffrin topped the first run in search of her first giant slalom victory since December 2023 and a record extending 111th overall, but she had to settle for seventh in increasing snowfall and bad visibility. Swedish ace Lara Hector dropped from second to fourth and Swiss Camille Rast from third to sixth. Shiffrin beat Aicher by 87 points for the overall title last season but has said that she will ski fewer races in her pet event, the slalom, this year and mainly focus on giant slalom and super-g. That could help Aicher who like in the past plans to contest all races across the four disciplines. She has five World Cup wins in downhill and super-g and slalom podiums, and now finally also a podium in giant slalom. The 2023 team event world champion Moltzan meanwhile celebrated her first ever win after 10 podiums in the past. "It feels like a fairy tale, pretty unreal. I can't imagine a better start," she said. "We have put in a lot of hard work in summer." Last year's Sölden and discipline title winner Julia Scheib crashed out in the first run in front of her Austrian home crowd. The men's season opening giant slalom is on Sunday on the same hill.

title: The Middleweight Adventure Bike That Delivers The GS Experience Without The GS Price - Top Speed
content: The GS badge has become shorthand for a serious adventure motorcycle, but that reputation comes with a premium price tag. BMW's F 900 GS combines a potent parallel-twin engine with off-road hardware and sophisticated rider aids, making it a natural benchmark for the middleweight ADV class. The question is how much of that performance you really need when your typical weekend involves winding back roads, the occasional gravel track, and a few hours in the saddle. There's a Japanese alternative that follows much of the same formula, including a 21-inch front wheel and spoked rims, while asking for considerably less of your wallet. The BMW F 900 GS makes a convincing case for its premium positioning with its 895cc parallel-twin being the heart of the package. It makes 105 horsepower at 8,500 rpm and 68.6 pound-feet of torque, which is plenty for a bike this size. It isn’t heavy, either. BMW lists the road-ready, fully fueled weight at about 482 pounds, helped along by a lightweight plastic fuel tank. The sticker is where it gets less fun. The F 900 GS carries a $14,495 MSRP plus $695 in destination, and that’s before you touch the options list or the accessory catalog. BMW also calls for premium fuel, so every fill-up costs a little more. Then there’s the bigger question. Plenty of riders spend most of their time on pavement and gravel, so a chunk of that capability never gets used. You still pay for it, though. That gap is exactly where a Japanese parallel twin with a 21-inch front wheel and spoked rims wants to live, at a much friendlier price. That bike is the Suzuki V-Strom 800DE. It’s Suzuki’s off-road-focused middleweight adventure bike, built around the same 776cc parallel twin that powers the GSX-8S. Don’t mistake it for a budget stand-in, either. The 2026 model carries an MSRP of $11,799, plus $700 destination. The F 900 GS lists at $14,495 plus $695. Do the math and the gap lands at $2,696, or about 18 percent of the BMW’s price. That’s real money. Even the base model gets most of the hardware covered below: the 21-inch front wheel, long-travel suspension, and a full electronics package. Want to load it up? The V-Strom 800DE Adventure lists at $13,249. It adds 37-liter aluminum side cases, an accessory bar, a skid plate, and remote-adjustable rear suspension. Even then, it still costs about $1,200 less than a base F 900 GS. Under the tank sits a liquid-cooled, DOHC 776cc parallel twin. Bore and stroke are 84 x 70 mm, compression is 12.8:1, and a six-speed gearbox sends power to the rear wheel via chain. A 270-degree crank gives it a V-twin-like feel, while Suzuki’s Cross Balancer (two counterbalancers set diagonally) keeps vibration down and the engine compact. Suzuki says it deliberately favored smooth, low-rpm torque over chasing peak power. The Suzuki produces a claimed 83 horsepower at 8,500 rpm and 57.5 pound-feet of torque at 6,800 rpm. That leaves it approximately 22 horsepower and 11 pound-feet behind the BMW. This naturally makes the F 900 GS the quicker motorcycle. Its additional performance should be noticeable during hard acceleration, highway passing maneuvers, and spirited riding with luggage or a passenger. However, peak output doesn't tell the whole story. Reviews of the 800DE have praised its tractable power delivery and the way its Gravel traction-control setting allows controlled rear-wheel slip. Owner discussions similarly highlight its versatility on highways and dirt roads. For riders who value usable performance over outright acceleration, the Suzuki's engine makes a compelling case. This is where the V-Strom really earns its keep. It rolls on a 21-inch front and a 17-inch rear spoked wheel, the same sizes as the BMW. Suspension travel is about 8.7 inches at both ends, with an inverted fork up front. BMW quotes 9.05 inches front and 8.46 inches rear for the F 900 GS, so it’s close to a wash. Ground clearance is 8.7 inches, the tallest in the V-Strom family. Suzuki even swept the muffler upward so it stays clear of all that long-travel suspension. That said, according to one reviewer, all that travel could mean a noticeable dive under hard braking that may take some getting used to. Weight is where you’ll notice a gap. The V-Strom’s curb weight is 507 pounds, while BMW lists 482 for the F 900 GS, fully fueled. Twenty-five pounds sounds small until you're picking it up out of a rut. Seat height tilts slightly in Suzuki’s favor. The V-Strom sits at 33.7 inches, against 34.2 inches for the standard F 900 GS. Half an inch might not sound like much, but it counts for shorter riders flat-footing at a stoplight. Suzuki covers the essentials well. The Suzuki Intelligent Ride System bundles three drive modes, traction control with a dedicated gravel setting, a rear-ABS-off option, and a standard bidirectional quick-shifter that leaves the clutch alone for most shifts. A five-inch color TFT display handles instrument duty. If you mostly want help on a dirt road, the Suzuki’s package covers the stuff that actually counts. Running costs tip toward Suzuki, too. Its 5.3-gallon tank also holds roughly 40 percent more than the F 900 GS’s 3.8 gallons, which helps when the next gas station sits a long way from the trailhead. The V-Strom’s weak spot is the warranty. Suzuki offers 12 months of limited coverage, versus BMW’s 36 months or 36,000 miles. That’s a real gap. Does the V-Strom 800DE give GS riders everything? Not quite. You give up some power, a few pounds, and warranty length. However, you keep the wheels, the travel, the clearance, and the electronics that matter off-road, and you keep $2,700 in your pocket. For plenty of weekend riders, that’s a trade worth making. title: GS Caltex Chairman Urges Tesla-Style Innovation Overhaul - 조선일보
content: Huh Tae-soo stresses digital foundation over AI additions, pushing structural overhaul at GS Caltex's DT Day event “There are two kinds of cars in the world: Tesla, and cars that are not Tesla.” These were the words spoken by Huh Tae-soo, GS Group chairman, on the 22nd during a meeting with employees of GS Caltex, the group’s flagship subsidiary. The remark positioned Tesla, an electric vehicle company that disrupted the internal combustion engine era, as a benchmark for innovation for a subsidiary that derives approximately 80% of its revenue from selling gasoline and diesel. Huh unexpectedly took the microphone at GS Caltex’s Deep Transformation (DT) Day event held at GS Tower in Gangnam-gu, Seoul. The DT Day is an internal forum for sharing innovation achievements. Huh stated, “While German automakers chose to add digital technology to existing internal combustion engine vehicles, Tesla designed its products from the ground up with digital technology as the foundation.” He added, “GS Caltex should not stop at adding AI to existing tasks but must rethink its workflows from the starting point.” The oil refining industry’s profitability is heavily influenced by international oil prices and petroleum product prices—external variables beyond a company’s control. Therefore, improving process efficiency is a key factor in competitiveness. Huh’s message is interpreted as a call for fundamental structural improvements beyond merely enhancing operational convenience through AI. Three years ago, Huh had visited the event for about 15 minutes and left without a message. This time, he stayed for over an hour, inspecting 15 exhibition booths one by one. He directly asked questions to young staff members and contributed ideas on-site. His belief is that employees who understand field operations best must accumulate experiences of identifying problems and solving them with AI to drive company-wide change. Huh emphasized, “We must connect tasks through digital means to respond to changes and create visible results.” Hur Sae-hong, GS Caltex vice chairman, who toured the event with Huh, said, “The challenges of each individual member come together to create the company’s innovation and future. When changes that transcend existing limitations at each position connect and spread, they will lead to GS Caltex’s growth.”

title: Who to Watch as Mikaela Shiffrin and the U.S. Women Return to Racing This Weekend - SKI Magazine
content: U.S. Alpine teammates Mikaela Shiffrin and Paula Moltzan are back on the slopes this weekend at Sölden. (Photo: Barbara Gindl/APA/AFP via Getty Images//Austria OUT) The FIS Alpine World Cup opener—a giant slalom on the Rettenbach Glacier above Sölden, Austria—can set the tone for the season ahead. Last year, the U.S. women made an emphatic statement, locking up six of the top 19 places. Paula Moltzan led the charge with a podium finish, while Mikaela Shiffrin finished fourth and Nina O’Brien sixth. The team carried that momentum through the 2025–’26 season, helping the United States capture the women’s Nations Cup for the first time ever. Awarded to the nation whose skiers accumulate the most World Cup points over the course of the season, the title reflected the depth of the U.S. roster, particularly in the technical events. Shiffrin and Moltzan combined for 16 World Cup podiums in slalom and GS, while O’Brien, AJ Hurt, Elisabeth Bocock, and Katie Hensien contributed valuable points. Now comes the question: Can the U.S. women do it again at this year’s World Cup opener, Oct. 24-25 on Sölden’s Rettenbach Glacier? The core of last year’s Sölden contingent is back, with the women who scored World Cup points at the opener returning to take another shot at the Rettenbach Glacier. Leading the charge is Shiffrin, who is putting renewed emphasis on giant slalom this season. Long dominant in slalom, she’s turning her attention to the event that upended her career two years ago. A crash in the 2024 Killington GS left her with a serious abdominal puncture wound. Returning to the discipline meant working through post-traumatic stress, but Shiffrin steadily rebuilt her confidence and climbed from 30th in the GS standings to fourth last season. Now, she’s ready to see how much further she can go. “I really wonder where I can take GS,” Shiffrin said earlier this fall. “I have a ton of questions about it in my own mind, and I want to find out.” Moltzan also finished last season on a high note, bookending her World Cup GS campaign with runner-up finishes in Sölden in October and Åre, Sweden, in March. Of her 10 career World Cup podiums to date, five came last season, four of them in GS. At 32, and entering her eighth full season on the World Cup circuit, Moltzan is looking for a fresh source of motivation. She made a major equipment change, joining VAN DEER-Red Bull Sports, the ski brand founded by eight-time overall World Cup champion Marcel Hirscher. The move offers her a chance to help shape the next generation of women’s slalom and GS skis. For Moltzan, the motivation goes beyond a new logo on her skis. “My route of inspiration is trying to develop this whole brand-new line of women’s equipment.” She spent the off-season testing skis to find the right set-up. While her ambitions remain high, she’s approaching the challenge with a little more patience.“I was truthfully not intending to switch ski brands this year after such an incredible season,” Moltzan said. “But the opportunity to develop and create a line of skis that I have a lot of influence on is something I’m really excited about.” O’Brien, 28, is chasing a milestone of her own: her first World Cup podium. She recorded a career-best fifth-place finish in GS before the 2026 Olympics, then delivered one of the Games’ standout GS second runs, posting the fastest time in the second run to climb from 29th to 20th overall. AJ Hurt, 25, who made her second Olympic team last winter, also returned to the GS top 10 last season after rehabbing a hip injury suffered when she straddled a gate in training in the early season. Katie Hensien, 26, will be looking to recapture the form that earned her a career-best fourth at Sölden in 2024. She too was injured early last season, fracturing her tibia after straddling a gate in training. Although Hensien qualified for the 2026 Olympics, she had to withdraw as she continued to recover. Then there’s Elisabeth Bocock, 21, one of the team’s rising young talents. She made her World Cup debut in 2023 and announced herself a year later by finishing the first run of the Killington GS in eighth place. Last winter, she appeared on track to earn her first Olympic team selection, but a string of DNFs in her primary event, giant slalom, ultimately derailed that bid. She still put together several top-15 World Cup finishes and closed the season with a silver medal in GS at the world junior championships. She also won her second national GS title last March. For Bocock, competing alongside some of the world’s best comes with its share of pressure—but also a built-in advantage. Training with Shiffrin, Moltzan, O’Brien, and the rest of the U.S. tech squad gives her a daily benchmark for what it takes to succeed at the highest level. “If you’re having a good day in training, if, say, you beat Paula or Nina, and you know that they win [World Cup] runs, you could be beating the entire world,” Bocock said. “But also, if you’re not skiing well, you can put it in perspective, like, okay, the people who are the best in the world are beating me. I will still be okay in the grand scheme of things. It can be reassuring while also kind of a motivator.” “My skiing ability has only benefited from having such a good team around me and pushing me to be better in training every day,” she added. “My career is at a higher level than it would have been if I was not surrounded by these girls.” The U.S. women arrived in Sölden last week after a globe-trotting offseason in search of consistent snow and quality training. The conditions weren’t always cooperative. As Bocock put it, “Europe was melting, in Chile it snowed an absurd amount, and in New Zealand, it was raining.” The result was a summer of adapting on the fly rather than stringing together long blocks of ideal training. “There wasn’t a massive block of good training days,” Bocock said, “but I’m still really excited. I think we got what we needed.” Not every day had to be about gates and split times, though. Moltzan remembered the powder skiing in Chile as a welcome change of pace. “We free skied powder for a couple of hours, then went to a place called Tío Bob’s, which is the après-ski spot in Portillo. Sometimes it’s good to have a great ‘life day.’” That balance could prove valuable as the team heads into another demanding winter. With Shiffrin embracing a new challenge, Moltzan exploring the possibilities of new equipment, and a deep supporting cast hungry to make its mark, the U.S. women have plenty of reasons to be optimistic. In previous years, you needed three streaming services to watch World Cup ski races. Finally, we only need one: U.S. Ski & Snowboard, NBC, and FIS have a new broadcast and streaming structure for the 2026-27 season. Every alpine World Cup and world championship will stream live on Peacock, and a new free YouTube channel and FAST channel—both called Ski & Snowboard World Cup. Tune in this weekend to watch the U.S. women kick off their World Cup seasons.

title: GS Caltex showcases AI-driven workplace innovations - The Korea Herald
content:
Business GS Caltex showcases AI-driven workplace innovations GS Caltex showcased a range of artificial intelligence-driven workplace innovations, from employee training tools to robotics and energy-saving initiatives, at its annual Deep Transformation Day held Thursday at GS Tower in southern Seoul. The fourth edition of the event, attended by GS Caltex Vice Chairman and CEO Hur Sae-hong and other executives and employees, featured 15 exhibition booths highlighting projects developed by staff to improve productivity and transform business operations. Among the initiatives were AI-powered training tutors using the Socratic method of questioning, applications of physical AI technologies such as drones, robots and smart helmets, and a multi-agent AI system designed to automate research report writing. The company also presented energy-saving projects at its Yeosu refinery, efforts to optimize catalyst procurement through data-driven decision-making and plans to overhaul its enterprise resource planning system. Other projects included a co-processing system for biofuel production, while outside experts discussed industrial AI, humanoid robots and changes in the global business environment. One highlight was the development of AI training tools inspired by digital and AI transformation technologies that Hur had shared internally. Employees adapted the concepts into several applications, including AiQ+, which integrates 12 job training courses in the company's Mobility & Marketing division, a Socratic AI tutor for junior production engineers and a finance training assistant. Under the theme "We," the event emphasized employee-led innovation and continuous improvement. "Each employee's challenges and initiatives come together to shape the company's innovation and future," Hur said. "When changes made by individuals are connected and spread across the organization, they can drive GS Caltex's growth." GS Group Chairman Huh Tae-soo, who also attended the event, stressed the need to redesign business processes around digital technologies rather than simply adding digital tools to existing operations. "We need to shift our perspective from applying digital technology to existing tasks to designing work and processes around digital technology from the outset," Huh said.
